title: The -me- slot: done, and the result still counts
goal: Tell "I ate earlier" from "I've already eaten", say "not yet", and use a slot that in Swahili can also mean a present state.
bekal: its negative with *-ja-*: *sijala* (I haven't eaten yet)
verbs that turn into states with *-me-*: *nimechoka*, *nimeshiba*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Karibu nyumbani
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon. Budi has been invited to dinner at Amina's family home for the first time.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Yes, I'm here. I brought a little fruit.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: Thank you so much! Have you eaten?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bado sijala. Nimekunywa chai tu asubuhi.
lines.id: Not yet. This morning I only had tea.
lines.literal: not-yet I-not-yet-eat. I-have-drunk tea only morning.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: Please, eat! Mom has made pilau.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Harufu nzuri sana! Nimeshiba kwa harufu tu.
lines.id: It smells wonderful! The smell alone has filled me up.
lines.literal: smell good very! I-have-become-full with smell only.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Baba hajarudi bado. Yuko kazini mpaka saa mbili.
lines.id: Dad isn't back yet. He's at work until eight.
lines.literal: father he-not-yet-return yet. he-is at-work until hour two.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Aa, nimesahau kitu... simu yangu iko wapi?
lines.id: Oh, I've forgotten something... where's my phone?
lines.literal: ah, I-have-forgotten thing... phone of-mine it-is where?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: It's on that table. You're tired, aren't you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kidogo. Nimetembea sana leo — nimeona mji wote!
lines.id: A little. I walked a lot today — I've seen the whole city!
lines.literal: little. I-have-walked very today — I-have-seen city all!

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Pole sana! Kaa, chakula kiko tayari.
lines.id: Poor you! Sit down, the food is ready.
lines.literal: patience very! sit, food it-is ready.

notes: **Hodi is the word for knocking.** You say it rather than knock, and the answer is always *karibu*. Even at a house with the door wide open, people call out *hodi* before going in — and a guest who knows to say *hodi* instantly sounds like someone who has lived here.

**Nimeshafika is -me- with -sha- slipped in.** That insert comes from *kwisha* (to finish) and means "already; well before now". *Nimekula* = I've eaten; *nimeshakula* = I've already eaten, so don't go to any trouble.

**Bado has two jobs.** As a one-word answer it means "not yet". Inside a sentence it goes with the *-ja-* form and can stand before or after it: *Bado sijala* = *Sijala bado*. It also means "still": *Bado ninasoma* (I'm still studying).
**Pilau is spiced rice**, a close cousin of pilaf — and its richer twin, *biriani*, is the very same biryani. The spices arrived by the same sea routes that brought Arabic words into this language.
**Mpaka means "until".** *Mpaka saa mbili* (until eight o'clock), *mpaka kesho* (until tomorrow), *kutoka... mpaka...* (from… to…). The same word also means "border".

grammars.title: -me-: done, and still felt now
body: Swahili has two kinds of past, and the difference isn't how long ago something happened but **whether its result still counts now**.
*Nilikula* = I ate (earlier; that story is over). *Nimekula* = I've eaten (so I'm full now — don't offer me more).

With -me-
The difference
rows: "I arrived at nine" vs "I'm here (it's me)"
"He went to bed early" vs "He's asleep now"
"I was tired yesterday" vs "I'm tired now"
"Mom cooked pilau" vs "The pilau is ready"
"I forgot at the time" vs "I've forgotten — I can't remember now"
"He put on a kanzu" vs "He's wearing a kanzu"

after: The last rows show something that surprises new learners: for some verbs, **-me- actually translates a present state**. *Amesimama* = he's standing (he stood up, and still is). *Amekaa* = she's sitting. *Amevaa* = he's wearing. *Nimeshiba* = I'm full. *Nimeelewa* = I understand now.

Because *-me-* marks a result that still holds, it's the slot you'll use most when visiting, shopping, and on the phone: *Nimefika* (I'm here), *Nimepokea* (I've received it), *Nimeelewa* (I understand), *Nimemaliza* (I'm done).

grammars.title: Not yet: the -ja- slot
body: The negative of *-me-* isn't "haven't done" but **not yet** — and the slot changes to *-ja-*.
after: The verb ending **doesn't change** — just like the negative past in unit 11. Only the two front slots are swapped. Short verbs drop their *ku-*: *nimekula* → **sijala**, *nimekunywa* → **sijanywa**, *amekuja* → **hajaja**. Don't mix this up with the negative present from unit 4 (*sili*, *sinywi*, *siji*): that's "don't", this is "not yet".
Three sentences you'll say again and again: *Sijaelewa* (I don't get it yet), *Sijui bado* (I don't know yet), *Bado hajafika* (he hasn't arrived yet).

The four slots you now have: **-na-** present, **-li-** past, **-me-** already, with negatives *si…i*, *siku…*, *sija…*. One more slot — the future — is waiting in the next unit, and it's the easiest of all.

blocks.text: *Nimepotea* is the sentence to memorize whole before you explore a town on your own. Follow it with *Ninatafuta…* (I'm looking for…) and *Unaweza kunisaidia?* (can you help me?).
Visiting someone in East Africa has its own sequence, and nearly all of it is short sentences you already have the pieces for.

**Bringing something is always welcome** — fruit, sugar, tea, or bread from a roadside stall. The sentence: *Nimeleta kitu kidogo* (I brought a little something). Hosts don't normally refuse, so don't be surprised if it's declined once before being accepted.

*Naomba niondoke* literally means "I ask that I may leave" — the politest way to take your leave, and a sentence pattern you'll take apart yourself in unit 14. Leaving without saying it seems abrupt; saying it and then sitting another ten minutes is perfectly normal.

exercises.prompt: Choose -li- or -me-, then write the full sentence.
items: Mom has cooked (the food is ready). → ____
Last year she studied in Kenya. → ____

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: Nimefika. — Amepika chakula. — Tumemaliza kazi. — Wamekula. — Umeelewa. — Chakula kimekwisha.
Sijala. — Hajafika. — Hatujamaliza. — Hawajaja. — Hujaelewa. — Sijaona daktari.
Nimefika. — Jana nilifika saa tatu. — Mama amepika. — Mwaka jana alisoma Kenya. — Nimechoka.
Umekula? — Bado, sijala. — Baba hajarudi bado. — Nimesahau kitu. — Nimeelewa. — Chakula kiko tayari.
Umefika mapema. — Bado sijala. — Mama amepika pilau. — Baba hajarudi bado. — Nimetembea sana leo.
